notes.meaning: Nebuchadnezzar set up a huge statue, about 90 feet tall and 9 feet wide. It was most likely a frame covered with gold plates, and the height probably included a tall base. In chapter 2 he was told he was the head of gold. Now he makes the whole image gold, as if his kingdom would never end, and he forgets the praise he had just given to Israel's God.

The king called every leader in his empire to the dedication, the ceremony that would set the statue apart for worship. Satraps were governors over large regions, and every rank below them came too. If the great men bowed, he expected the common people to follow. The officials stood ready to obey, showing they would approve whatever the king approved.

A herald told people of every nation and language what to do. When the music played, all must bow at once, or be thrown into a blazing furnace. The music was meant to draw them in, and the fire was meant to frighten them. The choice was simple: turn or burn. People who already worshipped many gods could easily add one more, but Jews who worshipped only the true God could not.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars argue that the Greek names of several instruments show the book was written much later than Daniel's time. Others answer that Greeks were already in the region long before.

notes.meaning: As soon as the music sounded, the whole crowd fell down and worshipped. Most people go wherever their senses and fears lead. The careless world can be drawn into almost anything by music, or driven to it by a furnace. We learn not to take up a religion just because rulers command it, but to ask what God wants.

Some Chaldeans came forward to accuse the Jews. The phrase means, word for word, that they "ate the pieces of" the Jews, a vivid way to say they tore into them with slander. They were driven by jealousy, because these foreign captives had been given high posts.

The accusers began with the usual flattering greeting, "May you live forever!" Then they reminded the king of his own law and its fiery punishment. Sweet words often come right before cruel plans. They spoke as if they only cared about the king's honour.

They named Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego and pointed out that the king himself had promoted them. This made the three look ungrateful and disloyal. Daniel is not named, perhaps because he was away or too high in the king's favour to be touched.

The king flew into a rage, yet he still had the three men brought to him. His question can mean "Is it on purpose?" Because he had favoured them before, he gave them a chance to explain themselves. A man who ruled many nations could not rule his own temper.

The king offered them a second chance: the music would play again, and if they bowed, all would be forgiven. If not, they would burn at once. Then he mocked: what god could save them from his hand? He had forgotten that he once called their God the God of gods. He sounded like Pharaoh and Sennacherib before him.

The three said they did not need to answer. Their minds were already made up, so there was nothing to debate. God's command against bowing to idols had settled the matter. When something is plainly wrong, we should not stop to argue with temptation. They spoke calmly, with no insults and no flattery.

The opening words are hard to translate. Older Bibles read them as "If it be so," meaning "if you throw us into the fire." Either way, the three were answering the king's challenge: their God is able to rescue them. They did not doubt His power. Whether God saved them from death or through death, He would free them from the king's hand.

"But even if He does not": they did not claim to know what God would choose, but they would stay faithful either way. They did not serve God only to be rescued. Like Job, they would trust Him even if He let them die. Standing firm earlier about the king's food in chapter 1 had prepared them for this bigger test.

The king's face twisted with fury. "Seven times hotter" means as hot as it could possibly be made. His anger defeated its own aim, because a hotter fire would only kill them faster. God used his rage to make the rescue even more striking.

The strongest soldiers tied the three up, and they were thrown in still wearing all their clothes. Those clothes would catch fire easily. Every detail, the tight ropes, the clothing and the heat, makes the miracle that follows even greater.

The fire was so hot that it killed the soldiers who carried the three men up to it. The executioners died while the condemned men lived. This shows how deadly the fire was and how great God's protection would be.
The three fell into the furnace, still tightly bound and helpless. The word "bound" is stressed on purpose. It sets up the surprise in the next verses, when they are seen walking free.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Greek versions of Daniel add a long prayer and song of the three men at this point, and Catholic Bibles include them. Protestants treat these additions as apocrypha, books outside the Bible.

notes.meaning: The king jumped up in shock and asked his advisers whether they had thrown in three bound men. They answered, "Certainly." God made the king's own counsellors confirm the facts, so no one could deny the miracle.

Now four men were walking in the fire, unbound and unhurt. The fire burned only their ropes, and God's promise in Isaiah 43:2 came true: "When you walk through the fire, you will not be burned." They walked calmly, waiting for God's time to bring them out. The fourth looked like a heavenly being, and those who suffer for God have His presence with them.

differ.view: The fourth man was the Son of God himself, Jesus appearing before he was born as a man, walking with His people in the fire.
The fourth was an angel God sent to protect and comfort them, as the king himself says in verse 28.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: From the lips of a king who worshipped many gods, "a son of the gods" simply means a divine being.

notes.meaning: The king came to the furnace door and called them "servants of the Most High God." To him this meant the highest of the gods, not yet the only true God. The three did not rush out on their own. Like Noah waiting in the ark, they waited until they were called.

The officials crowded around and checked the three men closely. Not a hair was singed, their clothes were unharmed, and they did not even smell of smoke. These officials were no friends of the Jews, which makes their witness all the stronger. What Jesus later promised in a spiritual way, that not a hair of your head will perish, happened here in plain fact.

other.label: Popular modern teaching
other.view: Some teachers read the story as a picture of the end times. The king stands for the Antichrist, the statue for the image in Revelation 13, and the three men for Israel.

notes.meaning: The king praised God for sending His angel to save servants who trusted Him. He admired them for defying his command and giving up their bodies rather than worship another god. Yet he called Him "their God," not his own. A miracle moved him, but without God's word his heart was not truly changed.

The king ordered that no one may speak against the God of these three men, on pain of death. He did not command people to worship this God alone, only to treat Him with respect. Still, the decree protected the Jews in exile and helped keep them from idols.

The king gave the three men back their posts and raised them even higher. Their return to office spread the news of God's power across the province. Like chapter 1, the story ends with God's faithful servants honoured.
